title: Static electricity
ks3: Electricity and electromagnetism: static charge, electrons, attraction and repulsion, electric fields
intro: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. Practise charges, moving electrons, attraction and repulsion, sparks and lightning.
description: Free KS3 Physics static electricity questions with answers: positive and negative charge, electrons, attraction and repulsion, electric fields, sparks and lightning. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: You rub a balloon on your jumper. What happens to the balloon?
questions.hint: Rubbing two materials together moves tiny charged particles.
questions.explain: Rubbing moves electrons from one material to the other, so the balloon becomes electrically charged.

questions.q: Two objects have the same type of charge. What happens when they are brought close together?
questions.explain: Like charges repel: two positives push apart, and so do two negatives.

questions.q: A positively charged object is brought near a negatively charged object. What happens?
questions.explain: Opposite charges attract, so the objects pull towards each other.

questions.q: What type of charge does an electron have?
questions.hint: Electrons are the particles that move when things become charged.
questions.explain: Electrons are negatively charged. Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.

questions.q: A balloon is rubbed on hair. Which particles move from one material to the other?
questions.hint: These are the tiny particles on the outside of atoms.
questions.explain: Only electrons move. Protons are held tightly in the centre of each atom and can't move off.

questions.q: A balloon gains electrons. What charge does it have now?
questions.explain: It has gained extra negative electrons, so it is negatively charged.

questions.q: A balloon is rubbed on someone's hair, and the hair loses electrons. What charge does the hair have now?
questions.hint: It now has more protons than electrons.
questions.explain: Losing negative electrons leaves more positive charge than negative, so the hair is positively charged. That is why it is attracted to the balloon.

questions.q: What do we call the region around a charged object where it can push or pull other charges?
questions.hint: Charged objects can act on each other without touching.
questions.explain: A charged object has an electric field around it. Other charges inside the field feel a force.

options: A huge spark caused by charge building up in clouds
questions.hint: Think of a tiny spark from a door handle, but much bigger.
questions.explain: Charge builds up in storm clouds. When there is enough, it jumps to the ground (or to another cloud) as a giant spark: lightning.

questions.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall that is not charged. Why?
options: The balloon pulls the opposite charges in the wall closer, so they attract
Gravity pulls it to the wall
questions.hint: The balloon's charge affects the electrons in the wall's surface.
questions.explain: The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall's surface away, leaving the surface slightly positive. Opposite charges attract, so the balloon sticks.

questions.q: You walk across a carpet, touch a metal door handle and feel a small shock. Why?
options: Charge built up on you flows away through the metal
The handle has a battery in it
questions.explain: Walking on the carpet charges you up. Metal is a conductor, so when you touch it the charge suddenly flows away, giving a tiny spark.

questions.q: A charged plastic rod is held near tiny pieces of paper. What happens?
options: The paper is attracted to the rod
questions.hint: It is like the balloon and the wall.
questions.explain: The rod's charge pulls opposite charges in the paper towards it, so the light pieces of paper jump up to the rod.
